voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.

beats.vo: On a January night in 1931, a Liverpool insurance man named William Wallace got a phone message at his chess club. A stranger — a Mister Qualtrough — wanted to meet him the next evening, about a policy.

The next night, Wallace searched for over an hour for the address Qualtrough had given him. Half a dozen strangers, a policeman, a tram conductor — all watched him hunting for a street that didn't exist.
He gave up and went home. There, in the parlor, he found his wife Julia — beaten to death.

Police decided Wallace had called himself — an elaborate alibi to cover a murder. He was convicted. Then, on appeal, judges ruled the evidence couldn't support it: the first time in English law a murder conviction was overturned outright.
Wallace walked free, and died a few years later, still under suspicion. No one else was ever charged. If he didn't make that call, whoever did was never found.
